lessons.title: Hand Bending with Bars and Brakes
lessons.body: Hand bending is the foundation of all sheet metal forming. You need a straight edge, a bending bar (also called a folding bar), and a sturdy workbench. In many African workshops, a piece of hard wood or a steel angle iron clamped to a table works as a simple brake. Start with a piece of mild steel sheet, 0.8 mm to 1.2 mm thick. Thicker sheets are harder to bend by hand. Mark your bend line with a scriber or chalk. Clamp the sheet between two straight edges, leaving the bend line just outside the clamp. Use a mallet or a hammer with a smooth face to tap the sheet over the edge. For a sharp 90-degree bend, tap evenly along the line, working from one end to the other. Don't hit too hard or you'll stretch the metal and cause cracks. For a 1 mm thick sheet, a bend radius of about 1 mm is fine. If you need a larger radius, use a pipe or rod as a form. To bend a hem (a folded edge), first bend to 90 degrees, then fold flat. Practice on scrap pieces first. In Africa, many artisans use a 'bar folder' which is a simple machine with a clamping bar and a folding leaf. You can make one from angle iron and hinges. Always wear glovesâsheet metal edges are razor sharp. After bending, check the angle with a square. If it's not 90 degrees, adjust your clamping or hit harder on the open side. Remember: bend lines must be accurate; a 1 mm error becomes a big gap in the final product. For roofing sheets, gutters, and ductwork, hand bending is still common because it's cheap and portable.

lessons.title: Box and Pan Brake Operation
lessons.body: A box and pan brake (also called a finger brake) is a hand-operated machine that lets you bend boxes, pans, and channels with sides that would hit the machine on a standard brake. The key feature is a set of removable 'fingers' on the clamping bar. You can remove or rearrange fingers to clear the already-bent sides. In a typical African workshop, a 1.2 m (4 ft) box and pan brake is common. It handles mild steel up to 1.5 mm thick. To operate: first, adjust the clamping bar so it holds the sheet firmly but doesn't mark it. Use the two large screws at the front. Set the bending leaf (apron) to the desired angle using the stop rod. For a 90-degree bend, set the stop at 90. Insert the sheet between the clamping bar and the bed, aligning your bend line with the edge of the fingers. Clamp down. Lift the bending leaf smoothly. Don't force itâif it's too hard, your sheet is too thick or the clamp is too tight. For a box, bend the two long sides first, then the two short sides. Remove middle fingers to allow the short sides to clear the already-bent long sides. Always check your first bend with a square. If the bend is not sharp, adjust the clamping pressure. If the bend is off-center, your bend line was wrong. Practice with 0.8 mm galvanized sheetâit bends easily and is cheap. Common products: electrical boxes, drip trays, roofing flashings, and ventilation ducts. Keep the machine clean and oil the pivot points weekly. Never bend wire or rod in a box and pan brakeâit will damage the fingers.

lessons.title: Press Brake Fundamentals
lessons.body: A press brake is a powerful machine that bends sheet metal between a punch (top tool) and a die (bottom tool). It can bend thick sheetsâup to 6 mm or moreâwith great accuracy. In Africa, press brakes are found in larger metal fabrication shops, often used for making truck bodies, storage tanks, and heavy brackets. The main parts: a bed, a ram that moves up and down, and a control system (manual, NC, or CNC). The punch is mounted on the ram; the die sits on the bed. The sheet is placed on the die, and the ram pushes the punch down, forcing the metal into the die opening. The bend angle depends on how far the punch goes down (the depth) and the die width. A common rule: for a 90-degree bend in 2 mm mild steel, use a die opening of 12 mm (6 times the thickness). The inside bend radius is roughly equal to the die opening divided by 5. So a 12 mm die gives about 2.4 mm radius. To set up: first, choose the correct punch and die for your material and thickness. Align them. Set the back gauge to position the bend line. For a 1 m long bend, you need a press brake with at least 1 m bed length. Always wear safety glasses and keep hands clear of the pinch point. Never bend a sheet shorter than the die openingâit will slip. Test on scrap. If the bend is not 90 degrees, adjust the ram depth. If the bend is not straight, check for worn tools or uneven clamping. Press brakes are dangerousânever operate without training. In many African vocational schools, a small 20-ton press brake is used for teaching.

lessons.title: Roll Bending and Slip Rollers
lessons.body: Roll bending forms gentle curves, cylinders, and cones from flat sheet. The machine is called a slip roller or roll bender. It has three rollers: one top roller that can be adjusted up and down, and two bottom rollers that are fixed. The sheet is passed between them, and the pressure from the top roller bends it into a curve. In Africa, slip rollers are used to make water tanks, grain bins, stove pipes, and curved roofing. A typical hand-cranked slip roller costs less than a press brake and is common in small workshops. To operate: first, adjust the top roller so it just touches the sheet. Then, tighten it gradually with each pass. For a cylinder of 300 mm diameter from 1 mm mild steel, start with the top roller about 5 mm down from the sheet thickness. Crank the sheet through. Then lower the top roller by 2 mm and pass it through again. Repeat until you get the desired curve. Always feed the sheet straightâif it goes in at an angle, you'll get a twisted cylinder. For a cone, you need a slip roller with a conical attachment or you must pre-cut the sheet into a fan shape. After rolling, the cylinder will spring back slightly, so over-roll by about 5%. To weld a seam, clamp the cylinder and tack weld. Slip rollers can also bend wire edges and form lips. Keep the rollers clean and oil the bearings. Never roll a sheet thicker than the machine's capacityâit will damage the rollers. Practice with 0.8 mm galvanized sheet. For a 200 mm diameter pipe, you need a roller with a top roller diameter of at least 50 mm. Safety: keep fingers away from the pinch point; use a glove on the feed side.

lessons.title: Curling, Crimping, and Beading
lessons.body: Curling, crimping, and beading are finishing operations that add strength, safety, and appearance to sheet metal edges. Curling rolls the edge into a loop, removing sharp edges and stiffening the sheet. Crimping creates a wavy pattern that allows two sheets to interlock, like on stovepipes. Beading forms a raised ridge or groove for rigidity or decoration. In Africa, these operations are done with hand tools or small machines. For curling, you can use a curling iron (a hand tool with a curved jaw) or a rotary machine. Start with a 10 mm edge. Clamp the sheet, then gradually bend the edge over a rod. Work along the edge with a mallet. For a full curl (a closed loop), bend to 180 degrees, then hammer flat. Crimping is done with a crimping toolâa plier-like tool with corrugated jaws. You squeeze it along the edge every 5 mm. For stovepipes, one end is crimped so it fits into the uncrimped end of the next pipe. Beading uses a beading machine with rollers that form a groove. You can also use a hand bead roller. For a 1 mm sheet, a bead depth of 2 mm and width of 5 mm is typical. Beads are often placed 20 mm from the edge. These operations are common in African metal shops for making buckets, funnels, and ventilation ducts. Always wear glovesâcurled edges can still cut. Practice on scrap. For a professional finish, keep your tools sharp and your movements steady. A well-crimped joint is watertight and strong.

lessons.title: Forming with Hammers and Stakes
lessons.body: Hammers and stakes are the oldest sheet metal forming tools. A stake is a heavy metal formâlike a T-stake, a hatchet stake, or a ball stakeâthat fits into a bench plate or a vise. You shape the metal by hammering it over the stake. This is called 'raising' or 'blocking'. In Africa, this technique is used to make bowls, scoops, funnels, and car body panels. You need a good hammer: a ball-peen hammer for general work, a cross-peen for stretching, and a mallet for soft forming. Start with a flat sheet, annealed if possible. For a bowl, place the sheet over a ball stake and hammer from the center outward in a spiral. Use light, even blows. The metal stretches and curves. Move the sheet as you go. For a funnel, use a T-stake and hammer the sheet into a cone shape. Always hammer on the stake, not in the airâthe stake supports the metal and prevents dents. For a sharp fold, use a hatchet stake. For a curved flange, use a blowhorn stake. Keep your hammer face polishedâa rough face will mark the metal. After forming, you may need to planish (smooth) with a flat hammer over a flat stake. This removes hammer marks. Anneal the metal if it gets hardâheat to red and cool slowly. Practice with 1 mm copper or aluminum first; they are softer than steel. For steel, use 0.8 mm mild steel. Always wear safety glasses and ear protection. In many African workshops, old car leaf springs are used as stakes. A simple bench plate with various holes is a good start. This skill takes time, but it's the most versatile forming method.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a bending bar in hand bending?
options: B) To fold sheet metal over a straight edge
quiz.explanation: A bending bar is used to fold sheet metal along a straight edge.

quiz.q: Which tool is commonly used as a simple brake in African workshops?
options: B) A wooden block or angle iron clamped to a table
quiz.explanation: A wooden block or angle iron clamped to a table acts as a simple brake for hand bending.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum thickness for hand bending mild steel?
quiz.explanation: Hand bending is practical for mild steel up to about 1.2 mm thick.

quiz.q: What is a hem in sheet metal work?
options: C) A hole punched in metal
quiz.explanation: A hem is a folded edge that adds strength and removes sharpness.

quiz.q: Why should you wear gloves when hand bending?
options: B) To prevent cuts from sharp edges
quiz.explanation: Sheet metal edges are razor sharp and can cause serious cuts.

quiz.q: What is the key feature of a box and pan brake?
options: A) It can only bend 90 degrees
B) It has removable fingers on the clamping bar
C) It uses a hydraulic pump
quiz.explanation: Removable fingers allow bending boxes and pans with sides that would otherwise hit the machine.

quiz.q: What is the typical capacity of a 1.2 m box and pan brake for mild steel?
quiz.explanation: A typical 1.2 m box and pan brake handles mild steel up to 1.5 mm thick.

quiz.q: When bending a box, which sides should be bent first?
quiz.explanation: Bend the long sides first, then remove fingers to bend the short sides.

quiz.q: What should you do if the bending leaf is too hard to lift?
options: B) Check if the sheet is too thick or clamp too tight
quiz.explanation: Difficulty indicates the sheet may be too thick or the clamp is over-tightened.

quiz.q: What is a common product made with a box and pan brake?
quiz.explanation: Electrical boxes are commonly made with a box and pan brake.

quiz.q: What are the main parts of a press brake?
quiz.explanation: A press brake bends metal between a punch (top) and die (bottom).

quiz.q: For a 90-degree bend in 2 mm mild steel, what die opening is recommended?
quiz.explanation: A common rule is to use a die opening of 6 times the thickness, so 12 mm for 2 mm steel.

quiz.q: What is the inside bend radius roughly equal to when using a press brake?
options: A) The die opening divided by 5
quiz.explanation: The inside bend radius is approximately the die opening divided by 5.

quiz.q: What is a safety precaution when operating a press brake?
options: B) Keep hands clear of the pinch point
quiz.explanation: The pinch point between punch and die is dangerous, so keep hands clear.

quiz.q: What is a common product made with a press brake in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Press brakes are used for heavy fabrication like truck bodies and storage tanks.

quiz.q: How many rollers does a slip roller have?
quiz.explanation: A slip roller has three rollers: one top and two bottom.

quiz.q: What is a common product made with a slip roller?
quiz.explanation: Slip rollers are used to form cylinders for water tanks and pipes.

quiz.q: Why should you over-roll a cylinder by about 5%?
options: D) To make it easier to weld
quiz.explanation: Metal springs back slightly after rolling, so over-rolling compensates for that.

quiz.q: What happens if you feed a sheet at an angle into a slip roller?
options: B) It gets a twisted cylinder
quiz.explanation: Feeding at an angle causes the cylinder to twist.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a slip roller's top roller adjustment?
options: A) To control the bend radius
quiz.explanation: Lowering the top roller increases pressure and decreases the bend radius.

quiz.q: What does curling do to a sheet metal edge?
options: B) Rolls it into a loop
quiz.explanation: Curling rolls the edge into a loop for safety and strength.

quiz.q: What is crimping used for?
options: A) To make a wavy pattern for interlocking
quiz.explanation: Crimping creates a wavy pattern that allows two sheets to interlock.

quiz.q: What is a typical bead depth for a 1 mm sheet?
quiz.explanation: A bead depth of about 2 mm is typical for 1 mm sheet.

quiz.q: Which tool is used for hand crimping?
options: A) A crimping tool with corrugated jaws
quiz.explanation: A crimping tool with corrugated jaws is used to crimp edges by hand.

quiz.q: Why are beads placed on sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: Beads add rigidity and strength to flat sheets.

quiz.q: What is a stake in sheet metal forming?
options: A) A heavy metal form for hammering
quiz.explanation: A stake is a heavy metal form that supports the sheet during hammering.

quiz.q: Which hammer is best for general sheet metal forming?
quiz.explanation: A ball-peen hammer is commonly used for general forming work.

quiz.q: What does 'raising' mean in sheet metal work?
options: B) Shaping metal over a stake with a hammer
quiz.explanation: Raising is shaping metal by hammering it over a stake.

quiz.q: Why should you anneal metal during forming?
options: B) To make it softer and easier to shape
quiz.explanation: Annealing softens the metal, making it easier to form without cracking.

quiz.q: What is planishing used for?
quiz.explanation: Planishing smooths the surface after forming by using a flat hammer over a flat stake.
